title: 12,700 Indian Tech Professionals Returned From the US in Nine Months, Xpheno Data Shows
excerpt: Returns on the India–US corridor rose from 7,200 in 2023 to 15,100 in 2025, and 2026 is on pace to approach that record — but with about 14,500 moving the other way, the flow remains two-way, and the figures are recruitment-data estimates, not a government count.
body:
• About 12,700 white-collar technology professionals returned from the United States to India between January and September 2026, according to staffing firm Xpheno's figures reported by The Economic Times — up from 7,200 in 2023 and 9,800 in 2024, and close to 2025's full-year 15,100.
  • The traffic is still two-way: about 14,500 professionals moved from India to the US in the same nine months, so returns are rising, not yet a reversal.
  • Xpheno's numbers are estimates built from recruitment data — candidate databases, recruitment systems and job boards — not a government count, and they are not limited to H-1B holders.
  • If you hold an H-1B: the $100,000 payment applies only to certain new petitions for beneficiaries outside the US without a valid H-1B visa — USCIS states it does not apply to previously issued valid visas or to holders travelling in and out of the US.

More Indian technology professionals are moving home from the United States than at any point in recent years — and the flow is now large enough to measure year by year. About 12,700 white-collar technology professionals returned from the US to India between January and September 2026, according to data from staffing firm Xpheno reported by The Economic Times and summarised by Beats in Brief. The same series counted 7,200 returnees in 2023, 9,800 in 2024 and 15,100 in 2025.

"On September 19, 2025, President Trump signed a proclamation imposing a $100,000 payment on certain new H-1B petitions."

Whether 2026 sets a record is still an open question, and the reporting is careful about it: with three months left, another 2,400 returnees would take the year past 2025's total, which would require about 800 returns a month against the roughly 1,411 a month recorded from January to September. A record is a projection, not a result.

What the numbers count — and what they do not

Scope matters here. Xpheno's estimates are built from recruitment-related sources — candidate databases, recruitment management systems and job boards — rather than a complete government count of migration between the two countries. They cover white-collar technology professionals moving along the India–US corridor, and they are not limited to H-1B visa holders. The figures also do not establish why any individual returned: the data cannot separate a worker pushed out by a layoff from one who chose Bengaluru for family, a startup, or a senior role. A separate Xpheno tracking exercise, based on LinkedIn movements and reported by Thoughtful India, put returns from all countries at about 205,000 white-collar professionals so far in 2026, with the United States the largest single source — a different, wider measure that should not be mixed with the US-corridor series above.

The corridor itself remains two-way. About 14,500 technology professionals moved from India to the US in the same January–September period, against 12,700 moving the other way. Thoughtful India's analysis of the broader flow makes the same point: departures still outnumber returns by roughly two to one, though that ratio has narrowed from three to one in 2023.

The policy backdrop

US immigration policy is one documented part of the backdrop. On September 19, 2025, President Trump signed a proclamation imposing a $100,000 payment on certain new H-1B petitions. USCIS states the payment applies to petitions filed at or after 12:01 a.m. Eastern on September 21, 2025 for beneficiaries outside the United States who do not have a valid H-1B visa, and that it does not apply to previously issued, currently valid H-1B visas or prevent current holders from travelling in and out of the US. Beats in Brief reported that in September 2026 the White House announced a further 12-month extension of the restriction, until September 21, 2027. Indians are the group most exposed to any H-1B tightening: they accounted for 71 percent of approved H-1B applications in fiscal year 2024, a figure cited in the coverage.

Job loss carries its own clock. Under general H-1B rules, a worker who loses a job may receive a discretionary grace period of up to 60 consecutive days, or until the end of the authorised validity period, whichever is shorter, to find another eligible employer or another lawful option. For some, the reporting notes, returning to India becomes the practical choice when that search fails; for others it is a planned move that policy only accelerated.

What returnees are coming back to

The pull side of the story is the scale of India's own technology sector. A Nasscom–Zinnov report released in July 2026 counted 2,117 global capability centres in India, operating across 3,728 units and employing about 2.36 million professionals, and valued the sector at $98.4 billion in FY2026. These are the India units where multinationals run engineering, product development, research, analytics, cybersecurity and AI work — the roles most likely to use experience gained in the US. Roughly one-third of 600 high-tech startups founded between 2016 and 2023 were started by returnees, according to the Observer Research Foundation research cited by Thoughtful India.

The landing is not uniformly soft. The Economic Times reporting highlighted that some returnees take home only about 25–33 percent of their previous US salary — an estimate reported for some professionals, not a universal outcome, and one that has to be weighed against living costs, taxes and benefits on both sides. The US market they are leaving is not collapsing either: the US Bureau of Labor Statistics projects employment for software developers, quality assurance analysts and testers to grow 15 percent between 2024 and 2034, with about 129,200 openings a year.

What this means if you are weighing the move

Nothing in these figures requires an H-1B holder in the US to do anything. The $100,000 payment does not fall on existing visa holders, and returns remain the smaller of the two flows. What the data does support is narrower and more useful: the return option is being exercised at a scale — 12,700 people in nine months on one corridor alone — that makes it a mainstream career path rather than an exception, and India's capability-centre sector is the main place returnees land. The next data point to watch is Xpheno's full-year count: past 15,100, 2026 becomes the record year the current pace points to; below it, the trend is still rising, just more slowly than the headlines suggest.
